title: A pilgrimage
hook: a journey to a holy place, near or far
tomorrow: what do you call a birthday you can't remember?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a retreat that got crowded out, and kept later on a mountain: come apart awhile. Today, people who leave home on purpose, on foot.

A maps app will always offer the fastest route. Nobody on a pilgrimage wants it. People walk for days to a holy place that a car could reach in an hour. And Christians honestly disagree about whether the place itself matters. So, does God care which road you walk to pray? Two answers, both from the Bible, and both still walked.
screen: `THE FASTEST ROUTE, REFUSED.` → `DOES THE PLACE MATTER?` → `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH WALKED.`

segments.voice: The first answer: the place matters, and so does the road. Luke says Jesus' family made the trip: “Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.” A psalm sings the setting out: “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.” Another psalm blesses the ones whose hearts are already traveling: “Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them.” Pilgrimage is a living custom for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and for others too: Jerusalem, Rome, saints' shrines, the walking routes to Santiago in Spain. The going is part of the prayer. The second answer: no spot is holier than another. A woman at a well asks Jesus which mountain is the right one for worship. He says, “the hour cometh, when ye shall neither in this mountain, nor yet at Jerusalem, worship the Father.” And: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.” Some Christians, including some Protestants, hold to this and stay wary of calling one place holy ground. Now the detail both sides keep, worth telling a friend: two disciples walking home to Emmaus, sad and arguing, and “Jesus himself drew near, and went with them.” No shrine at the end. A road, and company on it.
screen: `VIEW ONE: THE ROAD IS PART OF IT.` · `IN WHOSE HEART ARE THE WAYS.` · `VIEW TWO: IN SPIRIT AND IN TRUTH.` · `BOTH KEEP THE EMMAUS ROAD.` · then, large: `WALK TO PRAY.`

segments.voice: Walk slowly for about a minute, across a room or down a hallway and back, letting each step land before the next. If you pray, let the walking be the prayer; if not, let it be attention. Then sit for the rest of the time, and feel the place you've come to.
A pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, near or far, where the going is part of the prayer.
Your line: walk to pray. Some walk toward a holy place, and some just find company on the road. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox Christians, and others too, make pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, saints' shrines or long walking routes such as the one to Santiago; others walk to somewhere close, like the church where they were baptized, while some Christians prefer not to treat any one place as holier.

fork.setup: a guy at your retreat says, "God's everywhere, so walking to a chapel is pointless." give the pilgrim's best answer.
options: the chapel is the one place where God can really hear you.
the psalms bless a heart set on the road; the going is part of the prayer.
walking lowers stress, so it's good for you either way.
fork.reveal: the pilgrim's best case is Psalm 84: blessed are those in whose heart are the ways. his best case is John 4: spirit and truth. both still walk, like the Emmaus road.

chat.says: made it to both! now jake says walking to the chapel's pointless since God's everywhere. is he wrong?
options: Half right. Jesus says worship in spirit and truth, but the Psalms bless the road too. Walk it.
Totally wrong. God is closer at the chapel, so getting there is the whole point.
Totally right. Christians don't really do pilgrimages; the Bible never mentions them.
chat.meaning: Both views are Christian: John 4 says worship in spirit and truth, anywhere; the Psalms bless hearts set on the road. And on the Emmaus road, Jesus walked along.

pilgrimage.meaning: a journey to a holy place, made as prayer

Passover.meaning: the Jewish feast remembering freedom from slavery in Egypt

Santiago.meaning: Santiago de Compostela, a pilgrim city in Spain

Emmaus.meaning: a village near Jerusalem in Luke's Easter story

shrines.meaning: holy places tied to a saint or a sacred event
